Essay:

Why You Should Ask More Than One Person

Last spring I had to pick an elective for high school, and I asked my older cousin first. He told me to take computer science because "that's where the jobs are." I almost signed up right away. Then I decided to ask my art teacher, my best friend, and my mom too. They all gave me different advice, and in the end I understood my own choice way better than I would have after just one talk. That taught me a good lesson. Asking more than one person for advice usually helps you make a better and smarter decision. Getting a few opinions helps you see things you missed, balances out people's bias, and gives you a fuller and clearer picture of your choice.

The first reason to ask several people is that each person only sees part of a situation. Nobody has lived every life, so their advice comes from their own experience. My cousin loves computer science because he is great at math and he enjoys puzzles. His advice was honest and kind, and it fit him well. It just did not fit me as well. When I talked to my art teacher, she smiled and pointed out that I spend most of my free time drawing. She said the digital design class mixes art with technology, which sounded exciting to me. I had never even thought about that class. One person showed me one door, and the second person showed me a door I did not know was there. When you collect advice from different people, all the little pieces fit together into something closer to the whole truth.

The second reason is that everyone has some bias, even when they care about you and want to help. Parents may want their kids to pick the safe choice because they love them and want them protected. Friends may want you to pick whatever keeps you close to them, since they enjoy your company. A salesperson wants you to buy the thing they are selling. These people are not lying. Their wishes can still quietly shape what they say. Think about someone buying a used car. If they only ask the dealer, they will hear that the car is in great shape and a good deal. If they also ask a friend who is a mechanic and read reviews from other owners, they might find out that the car has a common transmission problem. By hearing from people who want different things, the buyer gets a fair and honest view and can make a wise choice.

Third, hearing different opinions makes you think harder about what you value. When two people you trust disagree, you have to ask yourself which reason makes more sense and what matters most to you. My mom told me to pick the class with the easiest grading so I could keep my GPA safe and strong. My friend told me to pick whatever sounded the most fun. I realized I had to decide for myself if I cared more about good grades or about enjoying the class. Thinking about that was hard at first. Answering it made me feel proud and confident about my final choice. A single piece of advice can make a choice feel easy, and it can also let you skip the real thinking that a good decision needs.

Asking more than one person also protects you from simple mistakes. Doctors know this well, which is why patients who need a serious surgery are often told to get a second opinion. A second doctor might read the same test results in a new way, suggest a safer treatment, or agree that the first doctor was right. Either way, the patient wins. If the doctors agree, the patient can move forward with more trust and hope. If they disagree, the patient has found an important question in time. The same idea works for smaller things too, like asking two teachers to read your essay before you turn it in. One teacher might catch a confusing sentence that the other teacher missed, and your essay gets even better.

Of course, asking too many people can get overwhelming, and in the end the choice still belongs to you. Advice is a helpful tool, and you still have to use your own judgment. The goal is not to count votes and go with the most popular answer. The goal is to collect enough good ideas to make a smart choice. It works best to ask people who know different things, like an expert, someone who has been through the same thing, and someone who knows you well and wants the best for you. That works a lot better than asking ten people who all think the same way.

In the end, I picked the digital design class, and it became my favorite class of the whole year. I loved every project, I made great friends, and I felt happy walking into that room every day. I would never have found it if I had only listened to my first piece of advice. Talking to several people helped me see more options, notice hidden bias, and understand what I truly wanted. Whether you are picking a class, a car, or a medical treatment, listening to more than one voice gives you the best chance to choose well and feel good about your choice.
